open-question.question: Several Codex behaviours the design rests on are unverified on this machine: whether PLUGIN_ROOT is set for the commands a skill runs, whether a plugin-shipped agent can be spawned by name, how a plugin's skills are invoked, and whether a finished subagent accepts a follow-up message. The only Codex account available is free tier, so each live run spends a scarce allowance. At what point in the milestone should these behaviours be established by live Codex runs?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: The source at the installed version and the no-model CLI subcommands settle the design-bearing behaviours before any dependent decision is recorded, at no cost to the free-tier allowance, and the two runtime-only behaviours left over are ones the design can avoid leaning on until the single verification run the goal already budgets.
open-question.alternative: This rejects the premise that these behaviours need live model runs to be established. Before the dependent questions are answered, the behaviours are settled as far as possible without a model call. Sources are the openai/codex source at the installed 0.159.3 version, and Codex CLI subcommands that call no model: codex plugin marketplace add and codex plugin add on a fixture, codex plugin list, and codex debug prompt-input, which renders the model-visible prompt input and so shows how installed plugin skills and agents are presented. The findings go into the starting state. The goal's end-of-milestone verification run is the only live session. It establishes most of the design-bearing behaviours (skill naming, agent registration, environment set for skill commands) before any decision, at no cost to the free-tier allowance. The source is also more authoritative than the documentation the starting state flags as unconfirmed. Some behaviours may not be settled by source reading or prompt rendering. Whether a finished subagent accepts a follow-up message, and how a model actually resolves a spawn by name, are runtime matters, so those stay unconfirmed until the final run. Reading a large Rust codebase also costs maintainer time and can be misread.

Live runs come before the design is decided. Once the alternatives and recommendation passes have run, and before any of the dependent sibling questions is answered, a minimal throwaway fixture plugin is installed into Codex. It is not the cairn tree, which does not exist yet. One small live session then probes all four behaviours together: whether PLUGIN_ROOT is set in a skill's shell commands, whether a plugin-shipped agent can be spawned by name, how a plugin skill is invoked, and whether a finished subagent accepts a follow-up message. The results are added to requirements.md's starting state before the dependent questions are answered. Separately, the goal's live verification run still happens at the end of the milestone against the real tree. Every dependent decision (plugin-root literal, agent form and registration, skill invocation form, the repair branch of the alternatives pass) is recorded against observed behaviour rather than documentation the starting state marks as unconfirmed. This avoids the revert-then-re-answer cycles a wrong documented assumption would cause after tasks are derived. It spends free-tier allowance twice, once on the fixture probe and again on the final verification. A fixture plugin is also not the shipped tree, so a behaviour seen on the fixture can still differ on the real cairn tree, and requirements work stalls until a live session can be run.

The dependent sibling questions are answered now on documented behaviour and the evidence from the curated marketplace. derive-tasks puts one probe task at the head of the task list, run against a minimal fixture plugin before any task that builds on the probed behaviours. Any probe result that contradicts a recorded decision is handled by revert-then-re-answer of that decision before the dependent tasks continue. The final live verification run stays at the end of the milestone as the goal specifies. Requirements work goes ahead without waiting on a live session. Yet nothing is built on an unconfirmed behaviour, because the probe still comes before the implementation tasks it gates. Decisions are recorded on assumptions that may be overturned. A contradicting probe means reverting answers and possibly re-deriving tasks. It spends allowance on a separate fixture session as well as on the final run.

alternative.id: Just-in-time probes on the real tree

open-question.alternative: There is no up-front probe session. Each behaviour is checked by a small live run right before, or as part of, the task that depends on it, against the partially built hosts/codex/ tree rather than a fixture. The plugin-root probe runs once the host definition renders. The skill-invocation probe runs once the tree installs. The agent spawn and follow-up probes run once the agent form exists. Decisions are recorded on documented behaviour. The goal's final verification run happens at the end. Each probe exercises the real rendered artifact rather than a stand-in, so a pass is direct evidence for what ships. A failure surfaces exactly where it is cheapest to fix. It takes several separate live sessions, which is the most allowance-hungry pattern and the most exposed to hitting the free-tier limit partway (a condition the quota-exhaustion sibling governs). A late failure of an early-recorded decision, such as agent registration, can force rework of tasks already done.

No dedicated probe runs. The design is decided and built on Codex's documentation and the curated-marketplace evidence already in the starting state. The four behaviours are first established live by the goal's single end-of-milestone verification run (plugin install, one inline skill, one dispatch of each agent), and any mismatch it reveals is fixed then. It spends the least free-tier allowance: one live session in total, exactly the run the goal already budgets for. Every behaviour-dependent decision stays unconfirmed until the last step. If PLUGIN_ROOT is unset or plugin agents cannot be spawned by name, the fix may reshape the host definition, the agent form, and the dispatch-site wording after all tasks are done. The one run also has to carry both discovery and acceptance. The follow-up-message behaviour is only exercised if the run happens to hit the repair branch.

alternative.id: Non-model evidence, then a narrow live probe

open-question.alternative: First, before the dependent questions are answered, the behaviours are settled as far as possible without a model call: the openai/codex source at the installed version, plus codex plugin add, codex plugin list, and codex debug prompt-input on a fixture plugin. Then one small live session on the fixture probes only what that evidence left unsettled, typically follow-up messages to a finished subagent and spawn-by-name resolution. The results go into the starting state before the dependent questions are answered. The goal's final verification run happens at the end. Every dependent decision rests on confirmed behaviour, while the live probe is cut to the minimum the free-tier allowance has to pay for. It is the most up-front work before any requirement is answered: source reading, no-model CLI checks, and still a live session that must be scheduled. Requirements work waits on both. It also still spends allowance on a session separate from the final verification.

open-question.question: The live Codex verification runs on a free-tier account whose usage limit may be reached before the plugin install, the inline skill, and both agent dispatches have all been exercised. What should the milestone do if the limit stops the verification partway?
open-question.recommendation: It keeps the goal's full verification bar while spending the least quota, repeating only checks that have not passed, and it matches how a failed completion already leaves work resumable rather than redone.
open-question.alternative: The milestone stays open and nothing is finished or released while any of the four checks is still unrun. The four checks are the plugin install, the inline skill, and one dispatch of each agent. Evidence from the checks that already passed is kept as valid. When the free-tier limit resets, verification picks up at the first unrun check, and this repeats until all four have passed. It keeps the goal's full verification bar and spends the least quota on the way. Only checks that need the model are ever repeated: the install goes through `codex plugin` command-line subcommands rather than a model turn, and the passed checks are not run again. It also matches how a failed completion task already behaves, leaving the work in a state that can be resumed rather than redone. How long the milestone and the next release wait is decided by the account's reset schedule, not by the work. If the inline skill or an agent dispatch alone uses more than one window's allowance, the milestone can never finish on the free tier.

alternative.id: Full re-run after reset, hard gate

open-question.alternative: The milestone stays open and nothing is finished or released. Results from a stopped run are discarded. After the limit resets, the whole verification runs again from a fresh install as one unbroken run, and it counts only if all four checks pass inside that single run. The evidence comes from one build, one install, and one session. No pass is pieced together from runs that may have used different builds of the tree or different installed state. Every attempt spends quota on checks that already passed. A run that does not fit one window will fail the same way every time, so the gate can lock itself on the free tier. How likely that is depends on how much of the scarce allowance earlier live runs have already used, and when those runs happen belongs to the "Unverified behaviour probes" question.

alternative.id: Buy quota to finish now, hard gate

open-question.alternative: The milestone stays open and nothing is finished or released. Instead of waiting for a reset, the unrun checks are finished right away on extra capacity: a paid Codex plan, another account, or API-key billing. The checks that already passed are kept. The full verification bar is met without waiting on the reset schedule, so the release-ready end state arrives as soon as the work is done. The milestone takes on a cost and a dependency on another account, which the goal set out to avoid by sizing the run for a free-tier account. Only the maintainer can provide that capacity, so this step cannot run unattended.

After the limit stops a run, verification resumes at the first unrun check, but only for a fixed number of resets. If checks are still unrun after that, the milestone finishes and is released anyway. The unrun checks are recorded in the milestone's records as unverified, and the Codex README and installation text mark the capabilities they cover as not yet live-verified. Their verification moves to later work. It makes a real attempt at the full bar but caps how long the release can wait. Every outcome ends in a defined state, either fully verified or partial with the gap stated. It adds a time limit someone has to choose and keep track of. If the limit runs out, cairn ships a Codex host whose least-established behaviour, the agent dispatches that the limit is most likely to cut, may not work for the users who install it.

When the limit stops a run, verification ends there. The milestone finishes and is released with the checks that passed recorded as verified. The unrun checks are recorded as unverified in the milestone's records, and the Codex README and installation text mark the capabilities they cover as not yet live-verified. Live verification of those checks is left to a later milestone. Quota never blocks a release, so the Claude Code and Antigravity releases never wait on a free-tier Codex reset. Users are told plainly which Codex behaviour is unproven. The milestone gives up its own end state of a Codex host verified end to end. The checks most likely to be cut are the agent dispatches, which the whole design is least sure about, so the shipped host may be missing exactly the part that sets cairn's pipeline apart.

When the limit stops a run, verification ends there. The milestone finishes and is released, and the unrun checks are recorded as unverified only in the milestone's own records (its completed-task entries and decisions). The Codex README and installation text claim the same support as the other hosts and are not changed to note the gap. The user-facing docs stay uniform across hosts, and no caveat text needs removing later once the gap is closed. The published docs claim Codex behaviour that no one has run, and the only record of the gap sits in milestone files that a Codex user never reads.

When the limit stops a run, the milestone still finishes with its code and docs complete and the unrun checks recorded as unverified. The Codex tree is held back from distribution: `uHappyLogic/cairn-codex` is neither published to nor advertised until a later run completes the verification. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees are released as usual. No unverified Codex host reaches users, and the work on the other two hosts is not held up. The release skill lists every directory under `scripts/hosts/` and stops on a missing distribution repository. Holding back one host therefore needs either a change to the release skill or an empty or stub `cairn-codex` repository. The milestone also ends short of the release-ready state its goal names, and the root README's Codex installation section has to stay hidden or point at nothing.

alternative.id: No rule now, decide when hit

open-question.alternative: The milestone records no fallback in advance. If the limit stops verification partway, the maintainer chooses what to do at that moment, based on how far the run got. No time is spent on a case that may never happen, and the eventual choice can use what the partial run actually showed. Whatever runs the verification task, such as the `complete-task` agent or a headless chain, has no rule for this case, so it can only stop with a failure. The milestone's verification bar then stays unclear exactly when someone needs to know it.

open-question.question: The traffic-badge workflow in each distribution repository pushes with the TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret, a fine-grained token scoped to exactly the three existing repositories and kept in no local copy, so only the maintainer can extend it to uHappyLogic/cairn-codex and set the secret there. How should the milestone treat that maintainer-only step?

recommendation.option: Release pre-flight gate, one regenerated token

open-question.recommendation: The check sits where the missing-repository stop already is, just before a tree is published into a repository whose workflow needs the secret, names no host so it covers every later one, keeps the single-token convention with one expiry to watch, and puts no task in the list that the completion agent could only fail.

alternative.id: Release pre-flight gate, one regenerated token

open-question.alternative: The release skill gets a check in its step 2f host loop that names no host. For every distribution repository it checks that a TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret exists, using `gh secret list --repo uHappyLogic/cairn-<host>`. If the secret is missing, the skill stops and prints the maintainer's instructions without running anything, the same way it already handles a missing repository. Those instructions say to extend the one token to the new repository, regenerate it, and re-set the secret in every repository. The step itself happens at the first Codex release, not inside the milestone, and the milestone's task list holds no task for it. The CLAUDE.md Development note changes from three repositories to four. The check is enforced at the point where it matters, just before a tree is published into a repository whose workflow needs the secret. It names no host, so it covers every later host too, and it matches the skill's existing rule that provisioning is the maintainer's job, printed and never run. It only checks that a secret with that name exists. It cannot check that the token's scope covers the repository or that the token has not expired, so a stale secret passes. It also adds a check, and a set of printed instructions, to the release skill for every host on every release, while regenerating the token still means re-setting the three existing secrets.

The milestone's task list gets a task that only the maintainer can complete. In it the maintainer extends the existing fine-grained TRAFFIC_TOKEN to uHappyLogic/cairn-codex as a fourth repository. Because the token's value is kept in no local copy, the maintainer regenerates it and sets the new value as the TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret in all four repositories: cairn, cairn-claude, cairn-antigravity and cairn-codex. The step must be done before the milestone finishes, after the maintainer has created the repository. The CLAUDE.md Development note changes from three repositories to four. The release skill is not changed for this step. The milestone's own task list tracks the step, so the milestone cannot be finished while the codex badges are unwired. The one-token-on-exactly-the-listed-repositories convention stays intact, with a single expiry date to watch. Regenerating the token invalidates the secret already set in the three working repositories, so all three must be re-set in the same sitting or their daily badge runs start failing. The task also cannot be done by the complete-task agent, so complete-all-tasks would stop on it with FAILED unless it is ordered last or done by hand. It needs the repository to exist before release, which brings the maintainer's repository creation forward into the milestone.

The milestone's task list gets a task that only the maintainer can complete. In it the maintainer creates a second fine-grained token scoped only to uHappyLogic/cairn-codex and sets it as that repository's TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret. The token used by the three existing repositories is left as it is. The step must be done before the milestone finishes, after the maintainer has created the repository. The CLAUDE.md Development note now describes one token per scope instead of one token on exactly three repositories. The release skill is not changed for this step. The step is still tracked and must be done before the milestone finishes, but it never touches the working token or the secrets in the three existing repositories. The step stays a single secret set in a single repository. There are now two tokens with separate expiry dates to rotate. This breaks the documented single-token convention, and every later host would add one more token. Like any maintainer-only task, the complete-task agent cannot finish it, and it needs the repository to exist before release.

The release skill gets the same per-host TRAFFIC_TOKEN existence check in step 2f, names no host, stops when the secret is missing, and never runs the fix itself. Here the printed instructions tell the maintainer to create a fine-grained token scoped only to the missing host's repository and set it as that repository's secret, so each new host brings its own token. The step happens at the first Codex release, and the milestone's task list holds no task for it. The CLAUDE.md Development note describes the per-host token scheme. The repeatable release gate is combined with a step that never disturbs the tokens of repositories already working. Adding a later host becomes the same short, isolated step each time. Tokens and their expiry dates multiply with every host, and the existing three-repository token becomes the odd one out under the new scheme. The check still only proves that a secret with that name exists, not that it works.

alternative.id: Documented maintainer step, one regenerated token

open-question.alternative: The milestone writes the step down without enforcing it. The CLAUDE.md Development note and CONTRIBUTING.md `## Development` now name four repositories and describe how to extend the token to a new distribution repository, regenerate it, and re-set the secret in every repository. The milestone's task list holds no task for the step and the release skill gets no check. The maintainer does it whenever they choose, before or after the first Codex release. It is the smallest change that still leaves a correct, findable record of the procedure. Nothing is added to the release skill or to the task list that the automated runners would trip over. Nothing makes sure the step gets done. If it is missed, the published cairn-codex workflow fails every day, sending failure notices, and its badges and its row in the root README's adoption table show nothing. Regenerating the token still means re-setting the three existing secrets whenever the maintainer acts.

alternative.id: Documented maintainer step, separate codex token

open-question.alternative: The milestone writes the step down without enforcing it. The CLAUDE.md Development note and CONTRIBUTING.md `## Development` describe giving each new distribution repository its own fine-grained token, set as that repository's TRAFFIC_TOKEN secret. The token used by the three existing repositories is left as it is. The milestone's task list holds no task for the step and the release skill gets no check. The maintainer does it whenever they choose. It is the lightest, easiest step for the maintainer to carry out: one new token and one secret in one repository, with no risk to the existing badge runs and no new workflow machinery. Nothing enforces it, so a missed step shows up only as daily workflow failures and empty codex badges. The number of tokens to rotate grows with every host, moving away from the documented single-token convention.

The milestone ships the codex traffic-workflow template and the badge markup as the goal requires, but treats the token extension and the secret as entirely outside its work. Its only trace is an Out of Scope entry. The milestone's task list holds no task for the step, the release skill gets no check, and no contributor documentation is updated, so the CLAUDE.md note keeps describing three repositories. The maintainer handles the token later, at a time and in a way the milestone does not specify. The milestone's work stays strictly within what its runners can do and verify. It makes no decision on token design that later operational experience might overturn. The goal's claim that the milestone ends release-ready across the full surface becomes partly false. The published cairn-codex traffic workflow fails from its first scheduled run, its badges and adoption-table row stay broken until someone remembers, and CLAUDE.md is left out of date about which repositories the token covers.

open-question.question: Every rendered skill, agent, and shared procedure reaches the plugin's Python tools and shared procedures through a per-host literal that replaces the {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} placeholder: an environment variable on Claude Code, a workspace-relative path on Antigravity. Codex's documentation names a PLUGIN_ROOT environment variable, but nothing yet shows that it is set for the shell commands a skill runs or inside a subagent. What literal should the Codex host definition use for the plugin root?
open-question.recommendation: It is Codex's documented contract and the form its own curated plugins use in shell commands, a one-line setting with no build change that holds wherever the plugin is installed, where the cache-path options tie the tree to an undocumented layout and the placeholder option makes every call a model rewrite.
open-question.alternative: The Codex host definition sets plugin_root to the documented runtime variable ${PLUGIN_ROOT}. Every rendered tool call becomes python3 ${PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/<tool>.py and every shared-procedure reference becomes ${PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/<name>.md. There is no fallback, and core/ and the build stay unchanged. This is the same pattern Claude Code uses, with the variable name Codex's plugin build page gives first. It matches Codex's documented plugin contract and how its own curated plugins call bundled scripts (python3 $PLUGIN_ROOT/skills/... appears 16 times in the cached openai-curated marketplace). It is a one-line settings value with no build or core/ change. It keeps working wherever Codex installs or caches the plugin, whatever the marketplace name or version. No live run has shown that the variable is set for the shell commands a skill runs or inside a subagent. One curated plugin (mixpanel-headless) even tells the model to set PLUGIN_ROOT itself before running scripts, which suggests it may not be exported. Nothing shows Codex substitutes it into skill text the way Claude Code does. If it doesn't, the shared-procedure paths that are read with a file-reading tool, not run through a shell, reach the model unexpanded. Whether this works depends on the timing of the sibling question about live probes.

The Codex host definition sets plugin_root to ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, the legacy alias Codex's documentation lists for PLUGIN_ROOT. Every {{PLUGIN_ROOT}} placeholder in the Codex tree renders to the same literal as in the Claude Code tree. There is no fallback, and core/ and the build stay unchanged. For a plugin first built for Claude Code, this is the alias Codex itself provides, so cairn's tool calls and procedure references render the same text on both hosts. The Codex tree differs from the Claude tree only where other settings make it differ, which makes cross-host diffs and reviews smaller. It builds on a name the documentation calls legacy, which Codex can drop without notice, and no curated Codex plugin uses it. It has the same unproven exposure as the primary variable: nothing shows it is set for skill shell commands or inside subagents, or substituted into text the model reads. It also puts a Claude-branded name into the Codex distribution, where users read it.

The Codex host definition sets plugin_root to a shell parameter expansion that uses PLUGIN_ROOT when it is set and otherwise falls back to the absolute install-cache path of the installed plugin. The form is ${PLUGIN_ROOT:-$HOME/.codex/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/cairn/<version>}, with the marketplace name fixed by the install route and the version filled per release. The build gains a way to fill the version into the plugin_root literal. It hedges the one unverified behaviour the question turns on. Shell commands still work if PLUGIN_ROOT turns out not to be exported to a skill's commands or a subagent's, so a quota-limited live run is less likely to fail at the first tool call. About 85 references in every skill, agent, and procedure grow into a long expansion. Shared-procedure paths read with a file-reading tool cannot be expanded by a shell, so the model has to interpret the expansion. The fallback ties the tree to Codex's undocumented cache layout (~/.codex/plugins/cache/... as seen on this machine, which also moves if CODEX_HOME is overridden), to the marketplace name the sibling install-route question settles, and to a build change that touches the fixed settings and rendering contract.

The Codex host definition sets plugin_root to the absolute install location of the plugin with no environment variable: $HOME/.codex/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/cairn/<version>, the layout Codex uses for installed plugins on this machine. The build gains a way to fill the release version into that literal. It does not depend on whether Codex exports or substitutes any plugin-root variable, in skills or subagents. It names a concrete directory the model can pass to a file-reading tool as well as to a shell command. The cache layout is observed, not documented, and moves with CODEX_HOME. The path embeds the marketplace name, which the sibling install-route question owns, and the version, so every release changes the literal across the whole tree. That needs a build change, and a user who installs through any other route gets a tree that points at nothing. $HOME also expands only in a shell, not in a read path.

The Codex host definition sets plugin_root to a path relative to the consuming project's root, as the Antigravity definition does with .agents/plugins/cairn. The plugin is expected to sit at that fixed location inside the project (for example .agents/plugins/cairn or .codex/plugins/cairn). No environment variable is used, and core/ and the build stay unchanged. It follows the pattern that already works for a host with no proven plugin-root variable. The same plain relative path works in shell commands run from the project root and in file-reading tool calls. It does not depend on whether Codex exports PLUGIN_ROOT to skills or subagents, or on where Codex caches installed plugins. It only works if the plugin files actually sit at that path in every project, which a marketplace install into Codex's own cache does not provide. That makes it depend on the sibling install-route question. It breaks for commands run from a subdirectory or with a different working directory, and it puts a vendored copy of the plugin in each user's repository.

The Codex host definition sets plugin_root to a prose placeholder such as <plugin-root>, the form about 40 curated Codex plugin skills use. The model replaces it with the installed plugin's absolute path, worked out from where the loaded skill or agent file sits, before every command or read. No environment variable is relied on, and the build stays unchanged. It works whether or not Codex exports or substitutes any variable, and whatever the install location, marketplace name, or version. Once resolved, the absolute path serves shell commands and file reads alike, and it follows an idiom Codex's own plugins already use. No rendered command can run verbatim. Every one of about 85 call sites depends on the model substituting correctly each time, which is exactly the kind of runner rewrite cairn's literal-command rule exists to avoid. Nothing in core/ tells the model how to resolve the placeholder, so it relies on the model's inference or on host-specific wording (owned by the sibling wording-mechanism question). A subagent whose instructions are not loaded from a file in the plugin may have no path to resolve from, which depends on the sibling agent-form question.

The milestone does not fix the Codex literal now. It records that the literal is chosen by a live Codex run that checks which of the candidates (the PLUGIN_ROOT variable, its CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT alias, or a path) resolves in a skill's shell commands, in a subagent's shell commands, and in text the model reads. The host definition carries a provisional value until then. The choice rests on observed behaviour rather than documentation that the requirements already flag as unconfirmed. That avoids building and documenting a tree around a variable that turns out not to be set where cairn's tools need it. The task decomposition depends on an unresolved value, and a free-tier live run is spent before the tree is final. If the quota runs out before the probe, the question stays open. Whether this works depends on the sibling questions about when the unverified-behaviour probes run and what to do if the quota is exhausted.

open-question.question: The runtime layer under core/ is written once for every host, and the build applies only three text operations to it: plugin-root replacement, regex deletion, and frontmatter key stripping. Where a core/ sentence cannot read the same on Codex as on the other hosts, for example the two dispatch sites that name the Agent tool and a cairn:<agent> registry name, by what mechanism should the difference reach the Codex tree?
open-question.recommendation: Each variation point is named in core/ and the build fails on a host that leaves one unfilled, the existing hosts' values are today's exact wording so their trees render unchanged, and the one mechanism extends the substitution the build already trusts to every Codex difference instead of markers, hidden match rules, or duplicated skills.
open-question.alternative: The build gains a new operation: core/ carries named placeholder slots, in the style of `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}`, at each sentence or phrase that differs, and a new settings key holds each host's value for every slot. All three host definitions declare every slot. The Claude Code and Antigravity values are today's exact wording, so their trees can render byte-identically. The existing unfilled-placeholder check catches a slot a host fails to fill. Each variation point is explicit and named in core/, every host has to supply it, and a missing value fails the build. It extends the one substitution pattern the build already trusts and scales to later differences such as the context-file name or the skill invocation form. It changes build_hosts.py's fixed key set and every host's settings.toml. It splits sentences between core/ and three settings files, so a core/ editor can no longer read the full instruction in one place. Multi-line values in TOML are awkward to maintain. How many sites it ends up serving depends on how the context-file and skill-invocation questions settle.

The build gets no new mechanism. Neither core/ nor any host definition carries a per-host variant, so the Codex tree renders the same dispatch sentences as the other two hosts, naming the `Agent` tool, `subagent_type`, the `cairn:<agent>` registry name, and "the agent id the `Agent` tool returned". The Codex runner has to map that wording onto its own subagent-spawning facility. Nothing changes in core/, in build_hosts.py's fixed settings key set, or in the Claude Code and Antigravity trees. The build keeps its three text operations, and no machinery is added before a live Codex run shows that it is needed. The Codex tree tells the runner to call a tool and pass a registry name that may not exist on Codex. Whether a dispatch then succeeds depends on how the model reads the sentence, and the milestone's goal requires both agents to run as Codex subagents. Whether this works at all depends on the axis the agent-form-and-registration question owns: how a Codex agent is named and spawned.

This rejects the premise that the sentence cannot read the same on every host. Each such core/ sentence is rewritten once in capability terms, for example "dispatch the `complete-task` agent of this plugin as a subagent, with a prompt containing only…" and "a follow-up message to the same subagent where the host can continue one". Specific tool names, parameter names, and registry names are dropped. The build and every host definition stay as they are, and all three trees render the new wording. It follows the existing invariant that host-dependent sentences name the capability, never the host. It keeps one text per site with no variants to keep in sync, and it needs no build change or per-host data. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees lose the exact `Agent`/`subagent_type`/`cairn:<agent>` instruction that reliably steers their runners today, so their dispatch text changes and their behaviour has to be re-shown. Whether that is allowed depends on the bar the existing-host preservation question owns. Neutral wording also works on Codex only if Codex can spawn the agent from a description rather than a precise name, which the agent-form question owns.

open-question.alternative: Extend "Notation and flags" so that Codex is a third binary: - Name `codex exec "<prompt>"` as the Codex form of a line. - Give each flag its Codex counterpart or say it has none: the permission bypass maps to Codex's own approvals-and-sandbox setting, `--model` has a counterpart in `-m`, `--effort` has no flag, and `--add-dir` exists under the same name. - Extend the one-line swap rule so a line moves to Codex by changing the binary, dropping `--model` and `--effort` to run at the account's defaults (as every agy line already does), and replacing the permission flag. No chain gets a Codex line. Gives a Codex user a complete, mechanical way to translate every chain, using the same rule the page already uses for agy. The page avoids naming any Codex model or effort level that a free-tier account may not offer, and its chains stay one block each. Codex runs lose the page's effort tiers (high, xhigh, max), which the chains deliberately vary line by line. That gap is real, because Codex does accept a reasoning effort through `-c model_reasoning_effort=…`. The swap rule's permission mapping depends on how the "Codex sandbox requirements" question settles, and the prompt text depends on the "Codex skill invocation form" question. No `codex exec` line is shown to have been run.

Leave docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md as it stands, covering only `claude -p` and `agy -p`, with no Codex line, flag mapping, swap rule, or mention. Codex's headless form gets no documentation now. The page could gain Codex coverage in a later milestone, once a live headless Codex run has shown it works. Publishes nothing about Codex's headless form until it has been run. The milestone's free-tier live check covers only the plugin install, one inline skill, and one dispatch of each agent, never a `codex exec` chain. The page also stays exactly as it was tested. The milestone goal names Codex coverage in docs/ as part of being release-ready, and this is the only docs page that names host binaries (skill-reference.md mentions hosts only by capability). A Codex user would get no headless form, and the page's claim that a chain can mix hosts line by line would stay limited to two of the three supported hosts.

Add one sentence to the "Notation and flags" section saying that on Codex a headless run is `codex exec` with the prompt as its argument, and that its flags differ, pointing to `codex exec --help`. Add no flag-by-flag mapping, do not extend the swap rule, and add no Codex line to any chain. Every claude and agy line stays unchanged. Meets the goal's "Codex coverage in docs/" at almost no cost and with little that can go stale. The page claims only that `codex exec` exists, which the installed codex-cli 0.159.3 confirms. The user has to work out each flag alone: `-p` means a config profile on Codex, not a prompt, and there is no `--dangerously-skip-permissions` or `--effort`. These are exactly the points where a straight copy of a claude line fails. The note's prompt text depends on how the "Codex skill invocation form" question settles (`/cairn:<skill>` or `$skill`).

Extend "Notation and flags" as in the defaults variant (Codex as a third binary, each flag mapped, the swap rule extended to `codex`, no chain gets a Codex line), with one difference. The swap rule tells the user to carry the line's model and effort over to Codex: a Codex model id through `-m`, and the line's effort through the `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"` config override, with the legend listing the effort levels Codex accepts. Keeps the page's per-line effort tiers on Codex. This rejects the question's premise that Codex has no effort control: the installed binary has a `model_reasoning_effort` config key that `-c` can set for a single run. It relies on a config key and on effort levels that no live run on this machine has confirmed, and Codex model ids or effort levels may not be available on a free-tier account. It also brings in the `-c` mechanism, which the other two hosts do not use. The permission mapping and prompt text depend on the "Codex sandbox requirements" and "Codex skill invocation form" questions.

alternative.id: Codex lines in a chain at defaults

open-question.alternative: Do the legend extension at defaults (Codex as a third binary, each flag mapped, the swap rule extended to `codex` with `--model` and `--effort` dropped). Also put at least one literal `codex exec` line into the shipped chains, for example a Codex review line in "Running a mixed-agent requirements review", so that chain mixes all three hosts. The Codex lines run at the account's default model and effort. Every other line stays as it is. Shows a complete Codex line the user can copy, and shows the page's selling point, mixing hosts line by line, across all three supported hosts. Leaving out model and effort follows the existing convention for agy lines. Every Codex line on the page is a literal command that a reader will run as written, yet the milestone's planned live verification runs no headless chain. A wrong flag or prompt form would therefore ship as working documentation. The line's permission flag and prompt text depend on the "Codex sandbox requirements" and "Codex skill invocation form" questions.

alternative.id: Codex lines in a chain with explicit settings

open-question.alternative: Do the legend extension with explicit settings (Codex as a third binary, each flag mapped, the swap rule carrying the model through `-m` and the effort through `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"`). Also put at least one literal `codex exec` line into the shipped chains, for example in the mixed-agent review section. That line names a Codex model id and an effort level, the same way the claude lines name theirs. Every other line stays as it is. Gives Codex the same treatment the page gives Claude Code: a copyable line with a deliberate model and effort, so a three-host chain can still match the reasoning tier to the step. The shipped line names a Codex model id and an effort level that may not exist on a free-tier account and that no live run has exercised. The `-c` override is also a further thing to keep in step with Codex releases. The permission flag and prompt text depend on the "Codex sandbox requirements" and "Codex skill invocation form" questions.

Do the legend extension with explicit settings. Also give every chain on the page a Codex form: each section gets its own `codex exec` block beside the existing one, and every line carries a Codex model id through `-m` and that line's effort through `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"`. The swap rule stays only for building mixed-host chains. A Codex user gets every workflow as ready-to-run lines, with the same per-line reasoning tiers Claude Code users get, and never has to apply a translation rule. Roughly doubles the chain content. It also goes against the page's design of one chain per goal plus a swap rule, and every Codex block must be kept in step by hand whenever a chain changes. All of those lines go unrun under a free-tier budget. The permission flag and prompt text in each line depend on the "Codex sandbox requirements" and "Codex skill invocation form" questions.

Restructure the page so that the chains no longer name a binary per line. Each line states the skill plus a model tier and effort tier. A single table in "Notation and flags" maps those tiers, and the permission, workspace, and prompt forms, to concrete command lines for `claude -p`, `agy -p`, and `codex exec`. Codex effort maps through `-c model_reasoning_effort="<level>"`. The existing claude and agy literal lines are rewritten into this form. Adds Codex, and any later host, as one table column rather than more lines or swap-rule clauses. This removes the per-host duplication that the other options either accept or work around. This rejects the page's premise that every line is a complete invocation you can paste. The reader then has to assemble every command from the table, including the claude lines that work today. It also rewrites a page well outside what Codex needs, which matters under the goal's condition that the Claude Code and Antigravity surfaces keep their behaviour. The Codex column depends on the "Codex sandbox requirements" and "Codex skill invocation form" questions.

open-question.question: The alternatives pass dispatches one subagent per open question, all at once where the host allows parallel dispatch and one after another where it does not, with no cap. Codex runs subagents in parallel but limits how many subagent threads a session may hold open at once. How should the pass behave on a host that allows parallel dispatch only up to a limit?

recommendation.option: Sliding window at a stated cap

open-question.recommendation: It gives the pass a defined outcome on a question set larger than the cap without the runner having to provoke and interpret a refusal, uses every free slot as each return lands the way the pass already judges returns, and confines the change to the Codex tree so the other two dispatch exactly as written today.

alternative.id: Sliding window at a stated cap

open-question.alternative: Only the Codex tree's dispatch step names an explicit limit: keep at most the session's configured subagent thread cap in flight at once, as Codex's agents.max_threads setting or the default value the prose states. As each question's pipeline finishes (embedded and committed, or skipped after its one repair), its agent is closed and the next pending question is dispatched. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep the uncapped all-at-once wording unchanged. Repair by continuation is unaffected, because closing waits for the repair window to end. The runner is told the limit up front, so it never has to provoke and interpret a refusal. The other two host trees can stay byte-identical, because the difference is confined to the Codex tree. It needs a way to deliver Codex-only wording into a core/ step. That mechanism belongs to the Host-specific wording mechanism question, and the build today offers only plugin-root replacement, regex deletion, and frontmatter stripping. The stated number can also drift from the user's actual configuration (the setting is user-editable, and Codex refuses agents.max_threads when multi_agent_v2 is enabled). A stated value that is too high brings back the refusal it was meant to avoid, and one that is too low wastes parallelism.

The pass keeps its current wording: every surviving question is dispatched at once where the host can run several dispatches together, with no cap. Neither core/ nor the Codex host definition adds any wording about a thread limit, so on Codex the host's own limit decides what happens to dispatches beyond it. Spawns past the limit get Codex's "agent thread limit reached" refusal, the prose defines no handling for that refusal, and the runner deals with it however it chooses. No thread is closed explicitly. Nothing in core/, the build, or either existing host tree changes. This milestone's live verification dispatches the alternatives agent only once, so it never comes near the limit and the pass works as written for that run. The pass has no defined outcome when a spawn is refused. This milestone alone holds sixteen open questions, well above a typical cap such as the agents.max_threads value Codex reads from config.toml. A refused spawn may be misread as a failure and skipped, may be retried blindly, or may stall the run. If finished subagent threads keep counting against the cap until they are closed (the Codex binary has a close_agent operation), even the sequential arm would hit the cap partway through. That behaviour is unverified, and when to probe it is up to the Unverified behaviour probes question.

The dispatch step in core/ gets host-neutral wording: dispatch together as many questions as the host will accept. A dispatch the host refuses because its agent limit is reached is not a failure and not a skip. It stays pending and is dispatched again as soon as a running question's pipeline has finished (embedded and committed, or skipped after its one repair). Where the host keeps finished agents open, that question's agent is closed at that point, so the window slides one slot at a time. The prose states no number: the window's size is whatever the host accepts. On a host with no limit the refusal never happens and the wording reduces to today's all-at-once arm. Repair by continuing the same session keeps working, because an agent is closed only once its repair window is over. Codex parallelism is used fully up to whatever limit the user's own configuration sets. The prose needs no stated number and no Codex-only sentence, and it reads correctly on every host, so the Claude Code and Antigravity runs dispatch exactly as they do now. The dispatch sentence in core/ changes, so the Claude Code and Antigravity trees change in text though not in behaviour. Whether that is acceptable depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. The approach also depends on the runner recognising the limit refusal as distinct from an agent failure, and on Codex releasing a slot when an agent is closed. Neither is yet confirmed by a live run (see the Unverified behaviour probes question).

The dispatch step in core/ gets host-neutral wording: dispatch questions until the host refuses one because its agent limit is reached, or until none are left. The accepted dispatches form a wave. Each return in the wave is judged, repaired once if needed, and committed or skipped as it lands. When the whole wave is done, every agent in it is closed (where the host keeps finished agents open) and the next wave starts from the remaining questions. The prose states no number, and on a host with no limit the first wave holds every question, which is today's behaviour. The bookkeeping is simpler than a sliding window. The runner tracks one batch at a time and closes agents in one sweep at the end of each wave, while the prose still needs no number and no Codex-only sentence. Within each wave the slowest agent holds up the start of the next wave, so slots sit idle and the wall-clock time falls between a sliding window's and the sequential arm's. Like the sliding window, the wording changes the core/ text of every host tree, which depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. It also relies on the runner recognising the limit refusal and on closing an agent actually freeing a slot, both unconfirmed by a live run.

Only the Codex tree's dispatch step names an explicit wave size: dispatch up to the session's configured subagent thread cap (agents.max_threads, or the default value the prose states). Each return is judged, repaired, and committed or skipped as it lands. When the wave is done, its agents are closed and the next wave of up to the cap begins. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees keep the uncapped all-at-once wording unchanged. It is the most predictable capped behaviour. The runner knows each wave's size before dispatching, never needs to interpret a refusal, and closes agents in one place. The other two host trees can stay byte-identical. It combines the costs of both of its positions. Slots sit idle while the slowest agent of each wave finishes. It needs the Codex-only wording mechanism that the Host-specific wording mechanism question owns. And the stated size can drift from the user's configured cap or from what multi_agent_v2 enforces.

alternative.id: Capped hosts take the sequential arm

open-question.alternative: The existing sequential arm's condition widens, in host-neutral wording in core/, from "where the host cannot run several dispatches at once" to "where it cannot run several at once, or can run only a limited number". On such a host each question is dispatched, judged, repaired at most once, and committed or skipped before the next is dispatched. Its agent is closed once its question is done, where the host keeps finished agents open. No number is stated and no window or wave is tracked. It reuses an arm the pass already defines, which writes the same blocks and lands the same commits. It adds no new dispatch mechanism and needs no Codex-only sentence. At most one subagent thread is ever open, so the cap cannot be reached whatever the user's configuration, and the one open handle keeps repair by continuation trivial. Total token use is the same as a parallel run. It gives up Codex's parallelism entirely, so a large question set takes as long as the slowest serial run. The arm's condition sentence also changes the core/ text of the Claude Code and Antigravity trees, which depends on the Existing-host preservation bar question. And it still relies on closing a finished agent freeing its thread, which is unconfirmed on Codex.

This rejects the premise that the pass should adapt. The dispatch step stays uncapped and unchanged in core/ and in every host tree. Instead, cairn's Codex-facing instructions tell users to raise Codex's subagent thread limit (agents.max_threads in config.toml) high enough to cover the open questions a milestone can hold before they run the alternatives pass. The pass itself never closes threads and never handles a limit refusal. No runtime file changes on any host, so the existing trees are untouched. On a correctly configured Codex session the pass runs in the same all-at-once arm it uses on Claude Code, with full parallelism. Correctness rests on a user setting that cairn cannot check. A question count above the configured value brings back the undefined refusal, and the count a milestone can reach has no upper bound. The setting cannot be used at all once multi_agent_v2 is enabled (Codex rejects agents.max_threads alongside it), and the instruction adds another configuration step to the Codex installation path.
